solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Take foolish risks in drama, and shoot

parts.note: a drama is a play
'with' can stand for 'and', as in bread with butter
to shoot a gun is to fire it

explanation.surface: Someone takes reckless chances on stage and with a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is not a link word here: it supplies WITH.
explanation.definitionFit: To play with fire is an idiom for courting danger by behaving recklessly.

parts.note: to pose a question is to ask it

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word setter

explanation.surface: A solver asks the setter, at the end, about the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A poser is a difficult question or problem, a synonym for a puzzle.

clue.text: Lost for words as we crashed lorry

indicators.note: the words as we are smashed up and rearranged

parts.note: lorry is the British word for a truck

explanation.surface: A witness is speechless as their lorry crashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone awestruck is so filled with wonder that they are rendered speechless.

indicators.note: casing means wrapping around, so the phrase for moderates encloses the joint

parts.note: to water down something is to moderate or weaken it
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: A film moderates a scene showing a joint being encased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'casing' splits the phrase for moderates so the joint sits in the middle. Watership Down is the 1978 animated film about rabbits.
explanation.definitionFit: Watership Down is a well-known animated feature, adapted from Richard Adams's novel.

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece covering another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: that and which are interchangeable relative pronouns

explanation.surface: A description of the roofing material on a church.
explanation.definitionFit: Thatch is straw or reeds used as a covering for roofs.

indicators.note: arresting means catching and holding, so the word for dread holds the next word inside it

parts.note: dread is fear
weight is force, as in throwing one's weight about

explanation.surface: Fear of the police force arresting a boxer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arresting' reads as police action but is the containment signal; 'force' is the police in the surface, weight in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A featherweight is a boxer in one of the lighter weight divisions.

definitions.meaning: ... in Sussex is an ancient port, one of the Cinque Ports
... is a whiskey distilled from ... grain

explanation.surface: A drinker wonders whether to order an old port or a whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vintage port' reads as wine; here it means an old harbour town. Rye, in East Sussex, was a medieval Cinque Port, one of England's historic channel ports.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye is both a historic Sussex harbour town and a whiskey style made largely from rye grain.

indicators.note: nervously suggests jittery movement, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A Greek nervously eyes the food, perhaps wanting more.
explanation.definitionFit: Greedy means wanting more food than one needs, which is what gluttonous describes.

indicators.note: we're told signals that the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: something dispatched has been sent

explanation.surface: A bouquet has been sent off, so we hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bouquet' suggests flowers but here means a wine's smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouquet is the aroma of wine, a particular scent.

clue.text: Dabbler, pal, invested in gold rings, initially

indicators.note: invested in means put inside, so the word for pal goes into the letters for gold and rings

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
a pal is a mate

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of the word rings

explanation.surface: A dabbler's friend has put money into gold rings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invested in' places the pal between the two letters of the gold symbol, with the rings' initial following.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur dabbles in an activity without professional skill or commitment.

indicators.note: some means part of, so the answer is a part of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone examines the groove left by a wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A rut is a groove worn into the ground by repeated passage of wheels.

clue.text: Hurdler, perhaps, or chaser, unfortunately last of twelve

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things going wrong, so these letters are jumbled
last of takes the final letter of the word twelve

explanation.surface: A jump racer finishes an unlucky last of twelve runners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges OR CHASER into RACEHORS; E comes from 'last of twelve'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurdler is a horse running over hurdles, so it is one example of a racehorse.

clue.text: Awful racket in road crossing Hyde Park

parts.note: awful means rotten
a racket is a row, a loud noise

explanation.surface: Complaining about a dreadful din on a road through a London park.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyde Park is a large royal park in central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotten Row is the famous riding track running along the south side of Hyde Park.

parts.note: plus means added to, as in two plus two
Hotel is the radio-alphabet word for H

explanation.surface: An extra has been added to the hotel, making it luxurious.
explanation.definitionFit: Plush describes lavish, luxurious surroundings, as de luxe does.

clue.text: Speak, under pressure, in golf club

indicators.note: in a down clue, the word for speak comes under the other, so after it

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
to utter is to speak

explanation.surface: A golfer is told to talk while under pressure with a club in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A putter is the golf club used on the green to roll the ball into the hole.

parts.note: a blackleg, a strike-breaker, is called a rat

indicators.note: extremely takes the extreme letters of the word testy

explanation.surface: A strike-breaker is irritable and very touchy.
explanation.walkthrough: A blackleg is British for a worker who crosses a picket line.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratty is informal British for irritable and short-tempered.

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: A new television has been installed near the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A tavern is an inn or pub, where drink is served at a bar.

clue.text: Happen to get hold of seat

parts.note: to take something is to get hold of it
a seat is a place, as in a place at the table

explanation.surface: Someone happens to grab a seat.
explanation.definitionFit: To take place is an idiom for an event occurring.

indicators.note: hidden by means the answer is concealed within the following words

explanation.surface: A lone bird lost within a vast flock of starlings.
explanation.walkthrough: A murmuration is a swirling flock of starlings.
explanation.definitionFit: The emu is a large flightless Australian bird.

clue.text: Poe character, American good guy deprived of love

indicators.note: deprived of means losing something, so the following letter is taken out

parts.note: the hero is the good guy in a story
love is zero in tennis, hence O

explanation.surface: A Poe character is an American nice guy who has lost his love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deprived of' removes O from HERO, leaving HER.
explanation.definitionFit: Roderick Usher is the doomed protagonist of Poe's tale The Fall of the House of Usher.

clue.text: Looks round about — not a pretty sight

parts.note: to look at is to eye, so looks gives eyes
O is round in shape
re means about, as in business letters

explanation.surface: Someone glances around at something ugly.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is something unpleasant to look at, an ugly sight.

clue.text: Conceit, for example, obvious at the start

parts.note: EG abbreviates the Latin exempli gratia, for example

indicators.note: at the start takes the opening letter of the word obvious

explanation.surface: Vanity, for instance, is apparent from the outset.
explanation.definitionFit: Ego in the sense of self-importance means vanity or conceit.

indicators.note: adjusted means changed in arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The saddle strap is right once it has been adjusted.
explanation.definitionFit: A girth is the band fastened round a horse's belly to keep the saddle in place.

parts.note: to con is to deceive, so conning means deceiving
a tug is a boat that tows, so a tower in the jokey sense; the question mark flags the pun

explanation.surface: A sneaky tug boat is part of a submarine.
explanation.walkthrough: TOWER is read as 'one who tows', not a tall building.
explanation.definitionFit: The conning tower is the raised structure on a submarine from which it is steered.
